title: Engaging a Third Party to Nudge Us Toward Action
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short piece argues that leaders frequently know the right course but lack the push to act, and that an outside expert's validation supplies the missing resolve. It notes that consultants often recommend the very path the leader had already chosen, yet that confirmation, backed by data, is what converts conviction into action. The author uses the five-frogs-on-a-log allegory to make the point that deciding and doing are different things. The move is to reframe seeking outside counsel as a legitimate tool for courage rather than a sign of weak judgment.
points: Outside experts usually confirm what the leader already believes, and that confirmation is the real value they deliver.
The five-frogs allegory captures the gap between deciding and doing: four decide to jump and all five remain on the log.
Risk and the cost of charting a new course make leaders hesitant, so a nudge or even a shove can be the difference in major strategic decisions.
Leaders should not be shy about requesting an outside view if it helps them find the courage to act.
quotes: That’s why leaders commonly turn to third parties for support. Third parties with deep expertise, experience, and wisdom play a critical role. Armed with the assessment and view of an expert, leaders find the validation they need to act.

Most of the time, the outside expert recommends the exact strategy or pathway the leader had already landed on. But the confirmation is invaluable, largely because it gives leaders the resolve to act.

Management consultants are widely used to provide just such a push or nudge forward. In fact, many of the world’s largest consulting firms tell organizations and their leaders what they already know to be true but do so with the data that encourages them to act on their original conviction.
As any consultant will tell you, the answer is all 5. Because there is a difference between deciding and doing!
When it comes to major decisions, a new strategic direction, or a critical response, good leaders sometimes need the help of a third-party expert to validate their thinking.
Don’t be shy about asking for an outside view. Whatever it takes to find the courage to act is a good thing. A little nudge can sometimes make all the difference.
